1.init: comment t.nanmean - the average, skipping NaN
1.name: comment

2.name: text_block

0.name: block
0.value:
Averages the values of a tensor as t.mean does, but skips any NaN (not-a-number) values instead of letting them spoil the answer.

Real data has holes in it - a dropped frame, a sensor that lost tracking, a division by zero upstream - and those often arrive as NaN. NaN plus anything is NaN, so ONE missing value turns a t.mean into NaN. t.nanmean averages only the values that are there: the sum of the real values divided by how many real values there are.

A ROW OF NOTHING BUT NaN:
gives NaN - there is nothing to average. (t.nansum gives 0 instead.)

THE dim ARGUMENT:
With no argument the WHOLE tensor is reduced to one value. A number typed after the name (t.nanmean 0) chooses a dim to reduce along and adds a dim inlet and a keep_dims checkbox - the argument creates them, so a node made without one cannot be given a dim later. For a table, dim 0 gives one answer per column, dim 1 one per row; -1 is the last dim.

SYNTAX:
t.nanmean <dim: int>
Default: no dim - the whole tensor.

EXAMPLE:
t.nanmean 0

INPUTS and PARAMETERS:

tensor in:
The tensor. Every one that arrives is averaged and the answer sent - this is the only inlet that makes the node send. A list or a NumPy array is first turned into a float32 tensor on the cpu; a tensor is used as it is, on its own device, and the answer stays there. An empty tensor is ignored: nothing is sent.
Like t.mean it needs floats: an int64 or bool tensor is refused ("expected input to have floating point or complex dtype") - whole numbers cannot hold a NaN anyway.
With no NaN in it the answer is exactly what t.mean gives.

dim (inlet, only when an argument was given):
A whole number. Changing it does NOT send by itself; the next tensor uses it. A dim the tensor does not have (2 or more for a table, or 1 for a 1-D tensor) is an error: the console prints "Dimension out of range" and nothing is sent.

keep_dims (checkbox, only when an argument was given; default off):
Off, the reduced dim is removed: 6 by 8 reduced on dim 0 has shape [8]. On, it is kept with length 1: shape [1, 8] on dim 0, [6, 1] on dim 1. Keep it when the answer must line up against the original again - to subtract each row's mean from that row, for instance.

OUTPUTS:

output:
With no dim, one number; with a dim, a tensor of means with that dim removed (or kept at length 1). NaN only where a whole row or column was NaN.

READING THE DEMO:
t.rand makes 6 rows by 8 columns of values between 0 and 1; click its button for new ones. make_hole passes the tensor through untouched until you click the toggle: then the cell at row 2, column 3 becomes NaN (the heat_map writes it as nan). The slider starts at dim 1 - one answer per row - and goes through 't bang int' to both dim nodes, re-sending the held tensor. With the toggle off, t.mean and
t.nanmean agree everywhere. With it on, t.mean of everything turns to nan, and so does its answer for row 2 (the third cell of its strip);
every other row is unaffected. t.nanmean's answers stay numbers: row 2 is averaged over its 7 remaining values.

RELATED:
t.mean is the plain version. t.nansum and t.nanmedian skip NaN the same way for the total and the middle value. np.nanmean is the NumPy version.
